sections.overview: The long-arm octopus is a coastal, bottom-dwelling species of Northeast Asia and an important local fishery resource. Its placement within the large genus *Octopus* remains provisional in current cephalopod literature.
sections.identification: It has a relatively small body and long arms, the features reflected in its common name. The species can vary in appearance among localities, and its phylogenetic position is not settled.
sections.habitat: It lives on the seabed in coastal waters of China, Korea and Japan, especially on muddy shores and tidal flats.
sections.diet: The species has a studied trophic ecology, but the sources consulted here do not support a single detailed prey list or reliable diet proportions.
sections.behavior: It is benthic and supports coastal fisheries. Research on its growth, feeding and behaviour informs fishery management, especially as overfishing has been reported as a concern.
sections.reproduction: A Korean study found the main spawning period to be April–May. Timing and fecundity may vary with local conditions, so these results should not be treated as a range-wide calendar.
sections.ecology: The species remains provisionally assigned to *Octopus*: recent phylogenetic work suggests closer affinity to *Callistoctopus*, but further evidence is needed to settle its placement.
sections.conservation: It is commercially important, and a recent review reports concern about declining catches and overfishing. The sources consulted do not provide a global conservation assessment.
